map.title: How Iterator::map works
map.description: Turns every item into a new value with a closure; nothing runs until the iterator is used.

note.text: the closure runs once per item

slides.caption: map(|x| x * 10) puts every item through the closure and yields what it returns.
1 goes in, 1 * 10 = 10 comes out.
2 becomes 20.
3 becomes 30. Same number of items in, same number out, same order.
map is lazy: on its own it does nothing. The work happens when something pulls the items, like collect() or a for loop.

filter.title: How Iterator::filter works
filter.description: Keeps only the items for which the closure returns true.

slides.caption: filter asks the closure about every item. true means keep it, false means skip it.
1 % 2 is 1, not 0: false, so 1 is skipped.
2 % 2 is 0: true, so 2 is kept.
3 is odd: skipped.
4 is even: kept.
filter never changes an item, it only decides whether it passes. The **x is needed because iter() gives references, and filter passes a reference to those.

enumerate.title: How Iterator::enumerate works
enumerate.description: Pairs every item with its position, counting from 0.

slides.caption: enumerate keeps a counter and hands out (counter, item) pairs.
The first item gets index 0, not 1.
The counter goes up by one for every item: (1, "b").
(2, "c"). The last index is always the length minus one.
Use it in a loop as: for (i, x) in v.iter().enumerate() { ... }

zip.title: How Iterator::zip works
zip.description: Walks two iterators side by side and pairs their items; stops at the shorter one.

note.text: pairs items in the same position

slides.caption: zip takes one item from each side at the same time and makes a pair.
1 and "a" are both first: they become (1, "a").
2 and "b" become (2, "b").
The second side is empty now, so zip stops. 3 has no partner and is never used.

eq.text: the shorter side decides the length

slides.caption: zip stops at the shorter iterator without an error. Nothing is padded; extra items are simply left out.

filter_map.title: How Iterator::filter_map works
filter_map.description: Transforms and filters in one step: Some(x) keeps x, None drops the item.

note.text: keep only the strings that are numbers

slides.caption: The closure returns an Option. filter_map unwraps every Some and throws every None away.
"1" parses to the number 1: Some(1), so 1 is kept.
"x" is not a number: parse fails, ok() turns the error into None, and the item is dropped.
"3" parses to Some(3): 3 is kept.
filter_map(f) does what filter followed by map would do, without computing f twice.

chain.title: How Iterator::chain works
chain.description: Runs one iterator to the end, then continues with a second one.

note.text: first the left side, then the right side

slides.caption: chain glues two iterators together end to end. Both must yield the same type.
All items of the first iterator come first: 1, then 2.
When the first one is empty, chain switches to the second: 3, then 4.
Nothing is copied or allocated: chain just asks the second iterator once the first says it is done.

take.title: How Iterator::take works
take.description: Yields at most n items, then stops; it also makes endless iterators finite.

slides.caption: 1.. counts up forever. take(3) lets only the first 3 items through.
1 is the first item: taken (1 of 3).
2 is taken (2 of 3).
3 is taken, and the limit of 3 is reached.
take now stops asking for more. 4, 5 and the rest are never even produced.
take(n) is how you safely use an endless iterator. If there are fewer than n items, it simply yields all of them.

skip.title: How Iterator::skip works
skip.description: Throws away the first n items and yields the rest.

slides.caption: skip(2) discards items until 2 have gone by, then lets everything through.
1 and 2 are the first two items: both are skipped.
From now on every item passes: 3 …
… 4 and 5.
skip(n) counts items, it never looks at their values. Skipping more items than there are gives an empty iterator, not an error.

take_while.title: How Iterator::take_while works
take_while.description: Yields items while the closure says true, and stops for good at the first false.

note.text: stops at the first item that fails

slides.caption: take_while tests each item in order and gives up at the first one that fails.
1 < 3: true, 1 is yielded.
2 < 3: true, 2 is yielded.
5 < 3 is false: take_while stops here.
The last 1 is smaller than 3, but it is never looked at. take_while is not a filter.
Use filter to keep every item that passes; use take_while to stop at the first one that does not.

skip_while.title: How Iterator::skip_while works
skip_while.description: Skips items while the closure says true; after the first false, everything passes.

note.text: skip the beginning, keep the rest

slides.caption: skip_while drops items from the front as long as they pass the test.
1 < 3: skipped.
2 < 3: skipped.
5 < 3 is false: skipping ends, and 5 is yielded.
1 is smaller than 3, but the closure is no longer asked: it is yielded too.
skip_while only trims the front. It is the opposite half of take_while with the same closure.

map_while.title: How Iterator::map_while works
map_while.description: Maps items while the closure returns Some, and stops at the first None.

note.text: like take_while and map in one

slides.caption: map_while calls the closure on each item. Some(v) yields v; the first None ends everything.
"1" parses: Some(1), so 1 is yielded.
"2" parses: 2 is yielded.
"x" does not parse: None. map_while stops right here.
"4" would parse, but it is never reached.
Compare filter_map, which would skip "x" and still yield 4.

step_by.title: How Iterator::step_by works
step_by.description: Yields the first item and then every n-th item after it.

note.text: every 3rd item, starting with the first

slides.caption: step_by(3) always yields the first item, then jumps 3 ahead each time.
The first item, 0, is always yielded.
Jump 3 ahead: 3.
Another 3: 6.
And 9. The next jump would land on 12, past the end, so it stops.
step_by(1) changes nothing, and step_by(0) panics: a step of zero would never move.

rev.title: How Iterator::rev works
rev.description: Walks an iterator from the back to the front.

slides.caption: rev asks the iterator for items from its back end instead of its front.
The last item, 3, comes out first.
Then 2.
And finally 1.
rev does not copy or reverse anything in memory. It only works on iterators that can be read from both ends (DoubleEndedIterator).

flat_map.title: How Iterator::flat_map works
flat_map.description: Maps every item to an iterator and yields all of their items in a row.

slides.caption: For every item the closure returns an iterator; flat_map empties each one in turn.
"ab".chars() gives 'a' and 'b'; both are yielded.
"cd".chars() gives 'c' and 'd'.
map would give two iterators; flat_map flattens them into one stream of characters.

flatten.title: How Iterator::flatten works
flatten.description: Removes one level of nesting; also drops None values.

slides.caption: flatten takes an iterator of iterators and yields the inner items one by one.
The first inner list gives 1 and 2.
The empty list gives nothing; it simply disappears.
The last list gives 3.
Only one level is removed: [[[1]]] becomes [[1]]. On Options, flatten keeps the values of Some and drops None.

scan.title: How Iterator::scan works
scan.description: Carries a running state through the items and yields a value at every step.

slides.caption: scan starts with the state 0. For every item the closure may update the state and returns what to yield.
sum = 0 + 1 = 1; scan yields 1.
sum = 1 + 2 = 3; yields 3.
sum = 3 + 3 = 6; yields 6.
fold gives only the final 6; scan shows every step on the way. Returning None from the closure ends the iterator.

cycle.title: How Iterator::cycle works
cycle.description: Repeats an iterator forever; combine it with take.

slides.caption: cycle yields the items and, when they run out, starts again from the beginning. take(5) stops it.
First pass: 1, 2.
The end is reached, so cycle starts over: 1, 2 again.
A third pass begins with 1, and take(5) has its 5 items.
Without take, cycle never ends. On an empty iterator it yields nothing at all.

copied.title: How Iterator::copied works
copied.description: Turns an iterator of references (&i32) into one of values (i32).

slides.caption: iter() yields references into the array. copied() copies each value out, so you get plain numbers.
&1 is copied to 1.
&3 to 3. The array itself is not changed.
copied() works for Copy types such as numbers and char; for types like String use cloned(), which calls clone().

inspect.title: How Iterator::inspect works
inspect.description: Lets you look at each item as it passes, without changing it.

note.text: peek at items on their way through

slides.caption: inspect runs a closure for each item and then passes the item on unchanged. Handy for debugging chains.
1 passes: the closure prints it, then sum adds it.
2 passes: printed, then added.
3 passes: printed, then added.
The program prints 1 2 3 and the sum is 6. inspect never changes the items.

fold.title: How Iterator::fold works
fold.description: Combines all items into one value, carrying an accumulator from item to item.

slides.caption: fold starts with the value you give it (0) and feeds it, together with each item, into the closure.
Before the first item, acc is the starting value 0.
Item 1: the closure returns 0 + 1 = 1, which becomes the new acc.
Item 4: 6 + 4 = 10. No items are left, so fold returns acc.
fold can build anything: a sum, a String, a Vec. For plain sums, sum() is shorter.

reduce.title: How Iterator::reduce works
reduce.description: Like fold, but the first item is the starting value; returns an Option.

slides.caption: reduce takes the first item as its starting value and combines the rest into it.
The first item, 3, becomes the accumulator.
Next is 9: max(3, 9) = 9.
Then 4: max(9, 4) = 9.
The result is wrapped in Some, because an empty iterator has no first item and would give None.
Use reduce when there is no natural starting value; fold when there is (0 for sums, an empty String, ...).

note.text: the ::<i32> says which type to add up into

slides.caption: sum starts at zero and adds every item.
The total starts at 0.
Add 1 and 2: the total is 3.
Add 3: 6.
Rust needs to know the result type, hence sum::<i32>() or let total: i32 = ... .sum(). An empty iterator sums to 0.
product starts at one and multiplies by every item.
The running product starts at 1, so multiplying does not change the first item.
Times 2: 2.
Times 3: 6.
Times 4: 24.
An empty iterator gives 1. Large products overflow quickly: i32 cannot hold 13 factorial.

count.title: How Iterator::count works
count.description: Counts the items by going through all of them.

slides.caption: count pulls every item out of the iterator and only remembers how many there were.
h, e: 2 so far.
l, l: 4 so far. Equal items are counted every time.
o: 5. The iterator is now used up.
count consumes the iterator. For a Vec or slice, len() is instant; count() has to walk through everything.

last.title: How Iterator::last works
last.description: Returns the final item, walking through all the others.

slides.caption: last reads every item and keeps only the most recent one.
1 is read, then forgotten.
2 is read, then forgotten.
3 is read and nothing follows, so it is the result: Some(3).
The value is really Some(&3), a reference, because iter() yields references; println! shows it as Some(3). An empty iterator gives None.

nth.title: How Iterator::nth works
nth.description: Returns the item at position n, counting from 0, and consumes everything before it.

slides.caption: nth(2) skips 2 items and returns the next one.
Position 0, "a": skipped.
Position 1, "b": skipped.
Position 2, "c": that is the answer.
nth(0) is the first item. Asking past the end gives None. Calling nth(2) again would continue after "c".

max.title: How Iterator::max works
max.description: Returns the largest item, or None for an empty iterator.

slides.caption: max keeps the biggest item seen so far.
4 is the biggest so far.
9 > 4: the new biggest.
1 < 9: no change. The answer is 9.
(The 9 is a reference, &9, because of iter().) max returns Option because an empty iterator has no largest item. With equal maximums, it returns the last one.

min.title: How Iterator::min works
min.description: Returns the smallest item, or None for an empty iterator.

slides.caption: min keeps the smallest item seen so far.
4 is the smallest so far.
9 is bigger: no change.
1 < 4: the new smallest, and the answer.
(A reference, &1, printed as 1.) Floats (f64) have no min() because NaN cannot be ordered; use fold with f64::min instead.

max_by_key.title: How Iterator::max_by_key works
max_by_key.description: Returns the item whose computed key is largest.

slides.caption: max_by_key compares keys, here the length of each word, and returns the item with the largest key.
"kiwi" has length 4.
"banana" has length 6: the largest so far.
"fig" has length 3. The winner is "banana".
It returns the item, not the key. min_by_key works the same way for the smallest key.

min_by_key.title: How Iterator::min_by_key works
min_by_key.description: Returns the item whose computed key is smallest.

slides.caption: min_by_key computes a key for every item (here the first number of the pair) and keeps the smallest.
(1, "ann") has key 1.
(0, "bo") has key 0, smaller: it wins.
With equal keys, min_by_key returns the first such item (max_by_key the last).

any.title: How Iterator::any works
any.description: True if at least one item passes; stops at the first one that does.

slides.caption: any checks the items in order and returns true at the first match.
1 is odd: keep looking.
3 is odd: keep looking.
4 is even: any returns true immediately.
5 is never checked.
any on an empty iterator is false: there is no item that could pass.

all.title: How Iterator::all works
all.description: True if every item passes; stops at the first one that fails.

slides.caption: all checks the items in order and returns false at the first one that fails.
2 is even: so far so good.
4 is even.
5 is odd: all returns false immediately.
6 is never checked; the answer is already known.
all on an empty iterator is true: no item fails.

find.title: How Iterator::find works
find.description: Returns the first item that passes the test, as an Option.

slides.caption: find tests items in order and stops at the first match.
3 > 5 is false: keep looking.
8 > 5: found. find returns Some(8) right away.
10 also passes, but find has already stopped.
find hands back a reference to the item (&8, printed as 8). If no item passes, find returns None.

find_map.title: How Iterator::find_map works
find_map.description: Returns the first Some the closure produces.

note.text: the first string that is a number

slides.caption: find_map calls the closure on each item until it returns Some.
"a" is not a number: None, keep going.
"7" parses: Some(7). find_map stops and returns it.
find_map is find and map in one: it returns the converted value, not the original item.

position.title: How Iterator::position works
position.description: Returns the index of the first item that passes the test.

slides.caption: position counts from 0 and returns the index of the first match.
Index 0, "a": not it.
Index 1, "b": a match. The answer is Some(1).
position returns where, find returns what. None means no item passed.

partition.title: How Iterator::partition works
partition.description: Splits the items into two collections: those that pass and those that do not.

slides.caption: partition sends each item to one of two collections, depending on the closure.
1 is odd: it goes to the second collection.
2 is even: first collection.
3 → odds, 4 → evens.
Each collection keeps the original order.
You get a tuple (passed, failed), so write let (evens, odds): (Vec<i32>, Vec<i32>) = ... .partition(...).

collect.title: How Iterator::collect works
collect.description: Runs the whole iterator chain and gathers the items into a collection.

slides.caption: map on its own does nothing. collect pulls the items through the chain one at a time.
collect asks for an item: 1 goes through map and becomes 1.
It asks again: 2 becomes 4.
3 becomes 9, and 4 becomes 16.
The range is used up, so collect builds the Vec from the four items.
The target type decides what is built: Vec, String, HashSet, HashMap, even Result<Vec<_>, _>.

unzip.title: How Iterator::unzip works
unzip.description: Splits an iterator of pairs into two collections.

slides.caption: unzip puts the first part of each pair into one collection and the second part into another.
(1, 'a'): 1 goes left, 'a' goes right.
(2, 'b'): 2 left, 'b' right.
unzip is the opposite of zip. Name both types: let (nums, letters): (Vec<i32>, Vec<char>) = ...

for_each.title: How Iterator::for_each works
for_each.description: Calls a closure on every item, like a for loop.

note.text: a for loop as a method

slides.caption: for_each runs the closure once for each item and returns nothing.
total = 0 + 1 = 1.
total = 1 + 2 = 3.
total = 3 + 3 = 6.
for_each is handy at the end of a long chain; a plain for loop is often easier to read and allows break.

is_sorted.title: How Iterator::is_sorted works
is_sorted.description: Checks that every item is less than or equal to the next.

slides.caption: is_sorted compares each item with the one after it.
2 <= 2 ✓: equal neighbours are fine.
2 <= 5 ✓. Every pair is in order: true.
It stops at the first pair out of order and returns false. Empty and single-item iterators are sorted.

eq.title: How Iterator::eq works
eq.description: Compares two iterators item by item.

slides.caption: eq walks both iterators together and compares the items in the same position.
3 != 4: the iterators differ, so eq returns false.
Iterators of different lengths are never equal. Useful to compare a Vec with a range: v.iter().copied().eq(1..=3).

repeat.title: How iter::repeat works
repeat.description: An endless iterator that yields the same value again and again.

note.text: the same value forever; take stops it

slides.caption: repeat("ab") yields a clone of "ab" every time it is asked, without end.
The first item: "ab".
The same again.
And again. take(3) stops after three.
repeat(x).take(n) is a quick way to make n copies; vec![x; n] does the same for a Vec.

once.title: How iter::once works
once.description: An iterator that yields exactly one value.

note.text: add a single item to a chain

slides.caption: once(0) yields 0 a single time. It is useful for putting one extra item in front of or behind a chain.
once yields its one value, 0.
Then it is empty, and chain continues with 1 and 2.
once(x) is like [x].into_iter(), but needs no array.

successors.title: How iter::successors works
successors.description: Starts from a value and computes each next value from the previous one.

note.text: each item from the one before

slides.caption: successors yields the first value, then keeps calling the closure on the last value until it returns None.
The start, 1, is yielded.
1 < 100, so the next value is 1 * 10 = 10.
10 < 100: the next is 100.
100 < 100 is false: the closure returns None and the iterator ends.
successors is ideal for sequences like powers, Collatz steps or walking up a tree.

from_fn.title: How iter::from_fn works
from_fn.description: Builds an iterator from a closure that returns the next item.

note.text: the closure keeps its own state

slides.caption: from_fn calls the closure each time an item is needed. Some(v) yields v; None ends the iterator.
n becomes 1; 1 <= 3, so Some(1).
n becomes 2: Some(2).
n becomes 3: Some(3).
n becomes 4; 4 <= 3 is false: None, the iterator is finished.
from_fn turns any "give me the next one" logic into an iterator that works with map, filter and collect.

peek.title: How Peekable::peek works
peek.description: Looks at the next item without taking it.

slides.caption: peekable() wraps an iterator so you can peek at the next item before deciding to take it.
peek() shows 1 but leaves it in place.
next() then takes that same 1.
peek would now show 2.
peek is how parsers look ahead: check the next token, and only take it if it is the right one.

next_if.title: How Peekable::next_if works
next_if.description: Takes the next item only if it passes a test.

slides.caption: next_if peeks at the next item and takes it only when the closure says true. Repeat it to read a run of digits.
'1' is a digit: taken.
'2' is a digit: taken.
'a' is not a digit: next_if returns None and leaves 'a' in the iterator.
Collecting while next_if succeeds reads "12" and stops before "a", which is still there for the next step.

max_by.title: How Iterator::max_by works
max_by.description: The largest item according to your own comparison.

slides.caption: Floats have no max() because of NaN. max_by lets you say how two items compare; total_cmp orders every float.
1.5 is the largest so far.
3.2 is larger.
2.0 is smaller. The answer is 3.2.
min_by works the same way. For a key instead of a comparison, use max_by_key.

min_by.title: How Iterator::min_by works
min_by.description: The smallest item according to your own comparison.

slides.caption: The closure returns an Ordering (Less, Equal, Greater) for two items.
"bb" (2) is the smallest so far.
"a" (1) is shorter.
"ccc" (3) is longer. The answer is "a".
For a simple key like the length, min_by_key(|s| s.len()) is shorter.

rfind.title: How DoubleEndedIterator::rfind works
rfind.description: Like find, but searches from the back.

slides.caption: rfind starts at the end and walks towards the front.
3 is odd.
6 is even: found, and the search stops.
find would have returned 4, the first even number from the front.

rposition.title: How Iterator::rposition works
rposition.description: The index of the last item that passes the test.

slides.caption: rposition walks from the back, but the index it returns still counts from the front.
Index 3, value 3: no.
Index 2, value 1: yes. The answer is Some(2).
position would return Some(0), the first 1.

zip_fn.title: How iter::zip works
zip_fn.description: The free-function form of zip: pairs up two iterables.

slides.caption: iter::zip(a, b) is the same as a.into_iter().zip(b), but reads more symmetrically.
1 and "a" form the first pair.
2 and "b" the second.
Like the method, it stops at the shorter side.

try_fold.title: How Iterator::try_fold works
try_fold.description: Like fold, but stops early when the closure returns an error or None.

slides.caption: try_fold carries an accumulator like fold, but the closure returns Option or Result.
Start at 0.
100 fits in a u8.
100 + 200 = 300 does not fit: checked_add gives None.
try_fold stops right away; 50 is never added.
With Result, the first Err is returned. Safe summing without overflow panics.

cloned.title: How Iterator::cloned works
cloned.description: Turns an iterator of references into one of owned clones.

slides.caption: iter() lends &String items. cloned() clones each one, so you get owned Strings.
"a" is cloned.
"b" is cloned. The original Vec still owns its Strings.
For Copy types like numbers, copied() is the cheaper equivalent.

by_ref.title: How Iterator::by_ref works
by_ref.description: Borrows an iterator so an adapter can use part of it, and you keep the rest.

slides.caption: take(2) would normally consume the iterator. by_ref() lends it instead.
take(2) gets 1 and 2 through the borrow.
The iterator is still there and continues with 3, 4, 5.
Typical for parsing: read a header with by_ref(), then the body.

cmp.title: How Iterator::cmp works
cmp.description: Compares two iterators item by item, like words in a dictionary.

slides.caption: cmp walks both sides together until the items differ.
3 < 4: the left side is Less.
If one side runs out first, the shorter one is Less: [1, 2] < [1, 2, 0].

nth_back.title: How DoubleEndedIterator::nth_back works
nth_back.description: The n-th item counting from the end (0 = last).

slides.caption: nth_back skips n items from the back.
"d" is position 0 from the back: skipped.
"c" is position 1: returned.
For a slice, letters.get(letters.len() - 2) does the same without an iterator.

rfold.title: How DoubleEndedIterator::rfold works
rfold.description: fold, but from the last item to the first.

slides.caption: rfold starts with the last item.
Start with an empty String.
The last item "c" first.
Then "b".
Then "a".
fold would give "abc". iter().rev().fold(...) is the same as rfold.

repeat_n.title: How iter::repeat_n works
repeat_n.description: Yields the same value exactly n times.

slides.caption: repeat_n(x, 3) is repeat(x).take(3) in one call.
Once.
Twice.
Three times, then it ends.
It clones the value for all but the last item, which is moved out.

repeat_with.title: How iter::repeat_with works
repeat_with.description: Calls a closure again and again to produce each item.

title.text: let mut x = 1; repeat_with(|| { let v = x; x *= 2; v }).take(4)

slides.caption: repeat_with calls the closure for every item; the closure may keep state.
1, and x becomes 2.
2, then 4.
8; take(4) stops it.
Like from_fn, but it never ends on its own.

empty.title: How iter::empty works
empty.description: An iterator with no items at all.

slides.caption: empty() yields nothing. It is useful where a function must return some iterator.
There is nothing to yield.
count() is 0.
once(x) is the one-item counterpart.

next_if_eq.title: How Peekable::next_if_eq works
next_if_eq.description: Takes the next item only if it equals the given value.

slides.caption: next_if_eq is next_if with an equality test, perfect for optional symbols.
The next char is '-': it is taken.
'5' is still there for the next step.
If the next item is different, it is left in place and you get None.

fuse.title: How Iterator::fuse works
fuse.description: After the first None, always returns None.

slides.caption: Most iterators already stop forever, but the rules allow one to resume after None. fuse guarantees it will not.
The first item passes through.
The first None is passed on.
Anything after it is hidden: None.
Needed only when you call next() again after None and rely on the answer.

peekable.title: How Iterator::peekable works
peekable.description: Wraps an iterator so you can look at the next item without taking it.

slides.caption: peek() lends the next item; next() still returns it afterwards.
peek shows 1, which stays in the iterator.
next takes 1.
Now peek shows 2.
The basis of hand-written tokenizers and parsers.

size_hint.title: How Iterator::size_hint works
size_hint.description: A lower and an optional upper bound on how many items are left.

slides.caption: collect() uses the hint to reserve memory in advance.
A range knows its exact length.
filter might drop everything: at least 0, at most 10.
An endless iterator reports (usize::MAX, None).

try_for_each.title: How Iterator::try_for_each works
try_for_each.description: Runs a fallible action on each item and stops at the first error.

slides.caption: The closure returns a Result; the first Err ends the loop and is returned.
"1" and "2" are fine.
"x" fails: try_for_each returns Err.
"4" is never looked at.
Return ControlFlow::Break to stop early without an error.

ne.title: How Iterator::ne works
ne.description: true if two iterators differ in any item or in length.

slides.caption: ne is the opposite of eq.
2 ≠ 3: different, true.
Slices and Vecs support != directly.

lt.title: How Iterator::lt works
lt.description: true if the first iterator comes first in dictionary order.

slides.caption: Items are compared pairwise until they differ.
"b" < "c": true.
le, gt and ge work the same; partial_cmp gives the full answer.

le.title: How Iterator::le works
le.description: true if the first iterator is less than or equal to the second.

slides.caption: Equal sequences count as "less or equal".
Every pair is equal.
Equal: true.
Same as !a.iter().gt(b.iter()).

gt.title: How Iterator::gt works
gt.description: true if the first iterator comes later in dictionary order.

slides.caption: The first difference decides, no matter the lengths.
2 > 1 already decides it.
The 9 is never compared.
Like words: "b" > "az".

ge.title: How Iterator::ge works
ge.description: true if the first iterator is greater than or equal to the second.

slides.caption: When one runs out first, the shorter sequence is the smaller one.
1, 2 match.
The second ran out: the first is greater.

partial_cmp.title: How Iterator::partial_cmp works
partial_cmp.description: Compares two iterators item by item; None if some items cannot be compared.

slides.caption: NaN cannot be ordered, so the comparison has no answer.
NaN vs 2.0: unordered, None.
Without NaN you get Some(Less), Some(Equal) or Some(Greater).

is_sorted_by.title: How Iterator::is_sorted_by works
is_sorted_by.description: Checks the order using your own rule for each pair of neighbours.

slides.caption: The closure says whether a may come before b.
Every pair passes: true.
Slices have is_sorted_by too.

is_sorted_by_key.title: How Iterator::is_sorted_by_key works
is_sorted_by_key.description: Checks that a key computed from each item never decreases.

slides.caption: Lengths 1, 2, 3.
Ascending: true.
Pair it with sort_by_key to check your own sorting.

next_back.title: How DoubleEndedIterator::next_back works
next_back.description: Takes the next item from the end.

slides.caption: A double-ended iterator can be consumed from the front and the back; they meet in the middle.
next() takes 1.
next_back() takes 3.
Only 2 is left.
rev() simply swaps next and next_back.

try_rfold.title: How DoubleEndedIterator::try_rfold works
try_rfold.description: try_fold from the back: stops early on None or Err.

slides.caption: It starts with 200 and stops as soon as the sum overflows.
200 + 100 = 300 does not fit: None, stop.
Same as iter().rev().try_fold(...).

len.title: How ExactSizeIterator::len works
len.description: The exact number of items left in the iterator.

slides.caption: Iterators over slices, ranges and Vecs know their exact length.
Before anything is taken: 4.
After one next(): 3.
filter() loses this ability, because it cannot know in advance.

once_with.title: How iter::once_with works
once_with.description: An iterator with one item, computed only if it is asked for.

slides.caption: once(x) needs x up front; once_with only runs the closure when the item is reached.
The Vec items come first.
Then the closure runs and yields 99.
If the chain stops early, the closure never runs.

peek_mut.title: How Peekable::peek_mut works
peek_mut.description: Looks at the next item and lets you change it before it is taken.

slides.caption: The changed value is what next() will return.
peek_mut lends the 1; it becomes 10.
The rest is unchanged.
Handy for merging or rewriting tokens on the fly.
